newsitem.title: USA: Scientists say too early to say if life on Mars.
newsitem.headline: Scientists say too early to say if life on Mars.

text.p: Scientists on Wednesday said it was too early to know if a meteorite that fell to Earth 13,000 years ago contained evidence of life on Mars.
A panel of experts in a news conference at Johnson Space Centre gave divided opinions about what had been found so far in research on the space rock.

"I think that one thing we can all agree on at this point is that it's really too early to come to a final conclusion about life on Mars. We're sort of in the discovery process for this," said Douglas Blanchard, chief of the earth science and solar system exploration division at the space centre.
The key area of dispute is whether structures on the gray rock are tiny fossils of Martian life or simply traces of inorganic processes forged in the Red Planet's harsh environment.
Some scientists say that the structures were formed at high temperatures, which would rule out life, but others disagree.

The possibility that the meteorite had Martian fossils was announced last August by a team of U.S. scientists. They said the meteorite was found in the frozen fields of Antarctica in 1984 and likely was blasted from the Mars surface 16 million years ago by the impact of an asteroid.

NASA planetary scientist Everett Gibson said he was increasingly convinced that the space rock shows evidence of life, and put the odds at better than 90 percent that his theory would be proven by the massive worldwide research effort currently under way.
"There are no show-stoppers to the ideas that we published last August ... We feel stronger about our position now than we did (then)," he said.
Gibson said there was evidence the structures in question had formed at low temperatures and were of sufficient size to be similar to single-cell life structures on Earth.

But scientist Ralph Harvey of Case Western Reserve University was sceptical. Some of the would-be fossils, he said, showed defects "that are characteristic of a high-energy (temperature) environment" and were "extremely consistent with an inorganic process."
But he also said that even if this meteorite -- officially known as ALH84001 -- turned out to have no signs of life, it would not "imply in any way that there is no life on Mars."

Laurie Leshin, a scientist from the University of California at Los Angeles, said if researchers finally determine the rock structures were formed in a high-temperature environment, then she would conclude that they were not traces of life. "But even if they are found to be low-temperature, it doesn't prove there was life," she said.
Blanchard said the August announcement had touched off an "explosion" of research on the meteorite and that 45 laboratories around the world had requested samples for study.
He said the investigative process had only just begun and could not predict when scientists would arrive at a consensus on whether the space rock showed there was life on Mars.
